Pure Seminoma Stages IIC and III 

Primary Treatment for Pure Seminoma Stages IIC and III 

outlined in Table 3 in Follow-up for Seminoma in the algorithm and 
includes a history and physical examination with optional measurement of 
post-orchiectomy serum tumor markers and imaging (abdomen/pelvis CT 
scan with contrast or MRI with and without contrast). The MRI protocol 
should include visualization of the retroperitoneal and pelvic nodes as well 
as all other nodes that need to be assessed. CT or MRI is not 
recommended beyond 5 years, unless clinically indicated. Chest x-ray is 
recommended and may be used for routine follow-up, but chest CT with 
contrast is preferred in the presence of thoracic symptoms. 

Follow-up for Pure Seminoma Stage II Post-primary RPLND and NOT 
Treated with Adjuvant Chemotherapy 

Patients with stage IIC or stage III seminomas are classified as either 
good or intermediate risk. All stage IIC and stage III seminomas are 
considered good risk except for stage IIIC disease, which involves non-
pulmonary visceral metastases (eg, bone, liver, brain) and is considered 
intermediate risk. Stage IIIB does not apply to pure seminomas. Standard 
first-line chemotherapy is used for both groups of patients. 

The recommended follow-up schedule for patients with stage IIA 
seminoma after RPLND not treated with adjuvant chemotherapy is 
outlined in Table 4 in Follow-up for Seminoma in the algorithm and 
includes a history and physical examination with optional measurement of 
serum tumor markers as well as imaging with abdomen/pelvis CT scan 
with contrast or MRI with and without contrast. The MRI protocol should 
include visualization of the retroperitoneal and pelvis nodes as well as all 
other nodes that need to be assessed. CT or MRI are not recommended 
beyond 5 years unless clinically indicated. Chest x-ray may be used for 
routine follow-up, but a chest CT with contrast is preferred in the presence 
of thoracic symptoms. 

Follow-up for Pure Seminoma Stage II After Primary RPLND and Adjuvant 
Chemotherapy 

For patients with good risk, three cycles of BEP or four cycles of EP are 
recommended (both preferred).127-129 The two regimens have not been 
compared head-to-head in patients with seminoma, so the Panel 
recommends that a number of factors be considered in choosing between 
the two. The specific schedule of the two regimens is different (9 weeks for 
three cycles of BEP compared to 12 weeks for four cycles of EP), which 
may make one more convenient for certain patients. While etoposide and 
cisplatin are associated with a dose-dependent increased risk of 
secondary cancers, there are no data addressing whether the risk is 
significantly higher with four cycles than with three. Bleomycin, which is 
cleared by the kidneys, is associated with a risk of pneumonitis and 
diminished pulmonary function. Therefore, four cycles of EP are generally 
preferable in patients with a reduced GFR (who would be expected to 
clear bleomycin more slowly), in patients >50 years of age (since renal 
function decreases with age), and in patients with COPD or other lung 
disease resulting in significantly diminished pulmonary function. Some 
oncologists prefer four cycles of EP for patients who smoke heavily 
regardless of lung function. The different risks associated with each 
regimen may lead individual patients to prefer one regimen over the other. 

The recommended follow-up schedule for patients with stage II seminoma 
after primary RPLND and adjuvant chemotherapy treatment is outlined in 
Table 5 in Follow-up for Seminoma in the algorithm and includes a history 
and physical examination and optional tumor marker assessment. 
Abdomen/pelvis CT with contrast or MRI with and without contrast is 
recommended, and the MRI protocol should include all nodes that need to 
be assessed. CT or MRI are not recommended beyond 5 years, unless

For patients with intermediate-risk disease, more intensive chemotherapy 
with four cycles of BEP (preferred) or four cycles of etoposide, mesna, 
ifosfamide, and cisplatin (VIP) is recommended.130-135 VIP should be 
reserved for patients with a contraindication to bleomycin (ie, a reduced or 
borderline GFR, aged >50 years, COPD, or other lung disease), but it 
should be kept in mind that this regimen is high risk for febrile neutropenia 
and granulocyte colony-stimulating factors (G-CSFs) should be used (see 
the NCCN Guidelines for Hematopoietic Growth Factors at 
www.NCCN.org). All of these chemotherapy options are category 1

recommendation.

tissue.136-140 FDG-PET can provide useful metabolic information on these 
lesions, which may aid in the early detection of recurrent disease in 
patients with normal CT findings, since functional abnormalities usually 
precede morphologic ones.140 However, testicular GCTs are typically slow-
growing and have low uptake of FDG on PET scans, often resulting in 
unclear images of testicular lesions.141 Additionally, the abdomen and 
retroperitoneal space are sites of non-specific FDG uptake, which can lead 
to false-positive results.141 Possible sources of false-negative results 
include small malignant lesions (<3 cm) and lesions with low proliferative 
indices.140 Therefore, accurate interpretation of FDG-PET scans is 
paramount and possible positive findings should not be based on FDG-
PET positivity alone due to its relatively low positive predictive value in 
residual lesions after chemotherapy.142 FDG-PET/CT is not indicated for 
residual masses ≤3 cm due to its low diagnostic accuracy in small 
tumors.140 To reduce the incidence of false-positive results due to 
inflammation, the FDG-PET/CT scan should be performed at least 6 
weeks after the completion of the last cycle of chemotherapy in patients 
with a residual mass >3 cm and normal serum tumor marker levels.140,143 A 
negative FDG-PET/CT following chemotherapy is very reassuring. If the 
FDG-PET/CT is negative or indeterminate, surveillance is recommended. 
If results are positive, imaging can be repeated in 6 to 12 weeks or 
resection or interventional radiology (IR)-guided biopsy of the residual 
mass should be performed. If imaging was repeated and the results are 
persistently positive, proceeding with resection or biopsy is recommended. 
For patients with a positive FDG-PET/CT, referral to a high-volume center 
should also be considered. 

If the residual disease is completely resected and histopathology shows 
viable seminoma, two cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy can be considered 
with the following regimens: EP, TIP (paclitaxel, ifosfamide, cisplatin),144 
VIP, or VeIP (vinblastine, mesna, ifosfamide, cisplatin).145,146 If the

Follow-up for Pure Seminoma Bulky Stage IIB, IIC, and Stage III After 
Chemotherapy 

The recommended follow-up schedule for patients with bulky clinical stage 
IIB, IIC, or stage III seminoma after treatment with chemotherapy is 
outlined in Table 6 in Follow-up for Seminoma in the algorithm and 
includes more frequent history and physical examination as well as 
optional measurement of serum tumor marker levels. Abdomen/pelvis CT 
scans with contrast or MRI with and without contrast are recommended, 
and the MRI protocol should include all nodes that need to be assessed. 
CT or MRI is not recommended beyond 5 years unless clinically indicated. 
Chest x-ray is recommended for routine follow-up; however, chest CT with 
contrast is preferred for patients with thoracic symptoms or residual 
masses or nodules in the chest. A chest CT with contrast should also be 
added in years 1 and 2 along with chest x-ray if supradiaphragmatic 
disease is present at diagnosis. Patients with residual masses may require 
more frequent imaging based on clinical judgment. An FDG-PET/CT scan 
of the skull base to mid-thigh can be conducted if clinically indicated. Since 
viable tumor cells have been found in tumors >3 cm with a negative post-
chemotherapy FDG-PET scan,148 the NCCN Panel recommends that 
patients with a residual mass measuring >3 cm and negative FDG-PET 

Nonseminomatous GCTs include nonseminoma tumors, mixed 
seminoma/nonseminoma tumors, and seminoma tumors in patients with 
elevated and continually rising serum AFP levels. To assess for metastatic 
disease, a CT scan with contrast or MRI with and without contrast of the 
chest, abdomen, and pelvis should be performed unless performed prior to 
orchiectomy. Use of FDG-PET/CT scan is not clinically indicated for 
nonseminoma.149,150 In select patients, brain MRI should also be 
performed; these patients include those with neurologic symptoms, post-
orchiectomy serum beta-hCG >5000 IU/L or AFP >10,000 ng/mL, 
predominance of choriocarcinoma, non-pulmonary visceral metastasis, or 
extensive lung metastases. Elevated levels of serum beta-hCG, LDH, or 
AFP should be followed up with repeated tests as TNM staging is based 
on post-orchiectomy values. In patients who had elevated serum tumor 
markers prior to orchiectomy, it is important to obtain the half-life kinetics 
of the tumor markers after orchiectomy if the markers are declining, 
because a slower-than-expected decline often indicates the presence of 
metastatic disease. The NCCN Panel emphasizes that mildly elevated, 
non-rising AFP levels may not indicate the presence of a GCT and that 
decisions to treat should not be based solely on AFP levels <20 ng/mL. 
Similarly, further workup should be considered before initiating treatment 
for mildly elevated beta-hCG (generally <20 IU/L) as other factors such as 
hypogonadism and cannabis use can cause false-positive results. 
Elevations of AFP either pre- or post-orchiectomy indicate the presence of 
nonseminomatous elements. The expected half-life for AFP is 5 to 7 days. 
For patients with elevated beta-hCG levels pre-orchiectomy, beta-hCG 
levels should be followed with repeated determinations after orchiectomy 
to determine their trajectory and, if declining, their nadir. The expected

half-life for beta-hCG is ≤3 days. For patients with normal imaging (ie, 
stage I), rising or persistently elevated beta-hCG levels generally indicate 
the presence of metastatic disease (stage IS). For patients with metastatic 
disease to the retroperitoneum or beyond (stage II and III), highly elevated 
beta-hCG levels (>1000 IU/L) may indicate the presence of non-
seminomatous tumor elements. Sperm banking should be recommended 
to patients of reproductive age, if clinically indicated, before undergoing 
any therapeutic intervention that may compromise fertility.39-42 Referral to 
social work, especially if factors exist that may affect follow-through of 
treatment (eg, lack of financial security, active military member where 
frequent moves or deployment is required) should also be considered. 

levels have three management options for primary treatment after 
orchiectomy: surveillance,51,59,152,153 nerve-sparing RPLND,154 or adjuvant 
chemotherapy with one cycle of BEP.155,156 The major difference in the 
treatment of patients at low risk and high risk is that surveillance is 
preferred for patients with stage I nonseminoma without risk factors, as it 
has been shown that the presence of risk factors, such as LVI, is a 
significant predictor of relapse when orchiectomy is followed by 
surveillance alone,33 whereas all three management options should be 
carefully considered when risk factors are present. It should be noted 
that surveillance or RPLND are also recommended options for patients 
with stage I pure teratoma and normal markers while RPLND is the 
preferred primary treatment option for patients with stage I GCTs with 
somatic type malignancy (previously referred to as transformed 
teratoma). The survival rates for stage I nonseminoma managed with 
surveillance, nerve-sparing RPLND, or one cycle of BEP chemotherapy 
exceed 98%. However, the high survival rate associated with 
surveillance depends on adherence to periodic follow-up examinations 
and subsequent chemotherapy for the 20% to 30% of patients who 
relapse. Therefore, patients who choose surveillance should adhere to 
the follow-up schedule. 

It should be noted that the Panel recommends staging tumors with 
discontinuous invasions of the spermatic cord as pT3 (high-risk stage I) 
and not as M1 (stage III) as is recommended in the 8th edition of the 
AJCC Cancer Staging Manual. It is critical to remember that risk of 
relapse to the pelvis is higher in these patients; thus, the pelvis should 
be included in imaging. Additionally, if a patient presents with mediastinal 
primary nonseminoma, this is considered poor-risk disease and should 
be treated with either VIP or BEP along with careful pulmonary 
functioning monitoring.151 

Nonseminoma Stage I with and without Risk Factors 

Primary Treatment for Nonseminoma Stage I with and without Risk 
Factors 

The NCCN Panel recommends treating patients with stage I 
nonseminoma based on the presence or absence of risk factors known 
to be associated with an increased risk of relapse (LVI, invasion of the 
spermatic cord, or invasion of the scrotum).46-54 Some centers also 
consider predominance of embryonal carcinoma as an additional risk 
factor for relapse. However, regardless of risk factors, patients with stage 
I nonseminoma with normal post-orchiectomy serum AFP and beta-hCG 

If nerve-sparing RPLND is chosen as primary treatment, it should be 
done within 4 weeks of a CT or MRI and within 2 weeks of repeat serum 
marker testing to ensure accurate presurgical staging.157 Referral to a 
high-volume center is recommended for patients undergoing RPLND. 
The goal of primary RPLND is cure. Dissection should include mass 
resection, lymphoid tissue around and behind the great vessels (ie, 
aorta, inferior vena cava) and the affected spermatic cord. The “split and 
roll” technique can be used to facilitate lymphoid tissue removal in which 
lumbar vessels are identified and sequentially ligated. Nerve-sparing 
approaches should be prioritized to minimize the risk of ejaculatory 
disorders in patients undergoing primary RPLND for stage I

based on the biology of the disease as well as the length of time on 
treatment should be considered along with an extension beyond 5 years at 
the discretion of the treating physician. Follow-up strategies for stage I 
nonseminoma are dependent on the presence or absence of risk factors 
as well as the treatment modality received. 

Follow-up During Surveillance 

nonseminoma. Limited data suggest increased frequency of aberrant 
recurrences with the use of minimally invasive laparoscopic or robotic 
approaches to RPLND. A recent case study of recurrence patterns in 
patients following robotic RPLND found that recurrences were highly 
variable, were in unusual locations, and were associated with a high 
treatment burden.158 However, two retrospective reviews on robotic 
RPLND done at experienced centers showed that this technique can be 
performed safely with low complication rates and similar oncologic 
outcomes to an open approach.159,160 Therefore, minimally invasive 
RPLND is not currently recommended as standard management, but can 
be considered in highly selected cases at high-volume centers. 

Long-term follow-up for patients with stage I nonseminoma without risk 
factors and for those with risk factors are outlined in Tables 7 and 8 in 
Follow-up for Nonseminoma in the algorithm. Both include a history and 
physical examination, serum tumor marker assessment, abdomen/pelvis 
CT scan with contrast or MRI with and without contrast, and chest x-ray at 
different intervals. These tests are more frequent in patients with risk 
factors. The MRI protocol should include visualization of the 
retroperitoneal and pelvis nodes as well as all other nodes that need to be 
assessed. Chest CT with contrast is preferred over chest x-ray in the 
presence of thoracic symptoms for patients regardless of treatment type 
as routine chest x-ray may have limited value for detecting relapse in 
patients with stage I nonseminoma. In a recent retrospective study, a total 
of 76 relapses were detected among 561 patients with stage I 
nonseminoma treated with surveillance following orchiectomy.112 All 
relapses were detected by either rising serum tumor markers and/or 
abnormal routine follow-up CT scans; no single relapse was detected by 
chest x-ray alone. Similar results have been reported in other studies, 
calling into question the value of chest x-rays in surveillance settings for 
stage I nonseminomatous GCTs.59,113,175 

For patients electing one cycle of BEP, imaging is also recommended 
within 4 weeks prior to the initiation of chemotherapy to confirm staging, 
even if scans were done previously. In a prospective trial by 
SWENOTECA, patients with stage I nonseminoma with or without LVI 
received one course of adjuvant BEP.156 The relapse rate at 5 years was 
3.2% for patients with LVI and 1.6% for patients without LVI. Five-year 
OS was 100% in both groups.46 The results after a median follow-up of 
7.9 years confirmed the low relapse rate with one course of adjuvant 
BEP, especially in patients with LVI.46 Several other studies using two 
cycles of BEP as primary treatment for patients with stage I 
nonseminoma have similarly reported relapse-free survival rates of 
>95%.153,161-165 However, late consequences of cisplatin-based 
chemotherapy, such as hearing damage and loss, cardiovascular 
conditions, hypertension, and neuropathy, have been reported during 
long-term follow-up.166-174 Therefore, one cycle of BEP is recommended 
due to its lower toxicity. 

Follow-up After One Cycle of Adjuvant BEP or Primary RPLND 

Follow-up for Nonseminoma Stage I with and without Risk Factors 

Follow-up of patients treated with either one cycle of adjuvant BEP or with 
primary RPLND is outlined in Table 9 in Follow-up for Nonseminoma in the 
algorithm and includes history and physical examination with testicular 
ultrasound for any equivocal exam, evaluation of serum makers, CT/MRI 

There is no single follow-up plan that is appropriate for patients with 
nonseminoma; however, the Panel has provided guidance for the first 5 
years after completion of therapy. Modifications for individual patients

of the abdomen and pelvis, and a chest x-ray. While the chest x-ray can 
be used for routine follow-up, chest CT with contrast is preferred in 
patients with thoracic symptoms. 

Nonseminoma Stage IS 

disease on imaging studies. These guidelines cannot address every 
possible situation, and the treatment of those rare patients with T any, N0, 
M0, S2–3 disease should be individualized; referral to a high-volume 
center is recommended. The vast majority of patients with stage IS have 
serum tumor markers in the S1 range, and they should receive first-line 
chemotherapy for good-risk disease: either three cycles of BEP or four 
cycles of EP (both preferred). Both regimens are category 1 
recommendations, and either is preferable to initial RPLND as these 
patients nearly always have disseminated disease.176,177 

Management of Nonseminoma Stage IS After Primary Treatment 

The treatment of patients with stage IS nonseminoma after primary 
treatment with chemotherapy is described below in Advanced Metastatic 
Nonseminoma (see Management of Good-, Intermediate-, and Poor-Risk 
Nonseminoma After Chemotherapy). 

Nonseminoma Stage IIA and IIB 

Primary Treatment for Nonseminoma Stage IIA 

Patients with stage IS nonseminoma exhibit highly elevated or persistently 
rising serum tumor markers post-orchiectomy, but no radiographic 
evidence of disease. However, mildly elevated levels of AFP or beta-hCG 
after orchiectomy must be interpreted with caution. Mildly elevated, non-
rising AFP levels (<20 ng/mL) may not indicate the presence of a GCT 
and should not be used to guide treatment decisions. In addition, 
hyperthyroidism, cannabis use, hypogonadism, and heterophile antibodies 
can result in significant elevations of beta-hCG.25-27,29,30 Elevated beta-
hCG due to metastatic disease typically rises steadily on serial 
measurements. In patients with mildly elevated but stable beta-hCG and 
no other evidence of metastatic disease, repeating the test using a 
different assay should be considered. Furthermore, many different 
conditions can result in an elevation of LDH, including many benign 
conditions. Therefore, patients should not be treated with chemotherapy 
for systemic disease if the only evidence of systemic disease is an 
elevation of LDH. 

Primary Treatment for Nonseminoma Stage IS 

The NCCN Panel recommends that patients with stage IS nonseminoma 
have a repeat scrotal ultrasound to rule out a contralateral testis mass if 
one has not been conducted in the last 3 months as well as be treated 
with first-line chemotherapy (see First-Line Chemotherapy Regimens for 
Germ Cell Tumors [TEST-E] in the algorithm) if the elevated marker is 
AFP or beta-hCG. For the purposes of this guideline, the NCCN Panel 
assumes that patients with stage IS disease have markers in the S1 
range. It would be extraordinarily rare for a patient to have an AFP >1000 
ng/mL or a beta-hCG >5000 IU/L and yet have no evidence of metastatic 

Primary treatment for patients with stage IIA nonseminoma depends on 
post-orchiectomy serum tumor marker levels. For patients with normal 
post-orchiectomy levels of AFP and beta-hCG, the NCCN Panel 
recommends either nerve-sparing RPLND or chemotherapy with three 
cycles of BEP or four cycles of EP as primary treatment options (both BEP 
and EP are preferred regimens).178,179 Chemotherapy is considered 
particularly appropriate if the patient has multifocal disease. RPLND is 
preferred as primary treatment for stage II tumors with somatic type 
malignancy (previously referred to as transformed teratoma). Referral to a 
high-volume center is recommended for those patients who undergo 
nerve-sparing RPLND. For patients with stage IIA seminoma with 
persistently elevated AFP and/or beta-hCG levels, the NCCN Panel 
recommends first-line chemotherapy with three cycles of BEP or four 
cycles of EP (both category 1; both preferred).154,180 For more information

below. A bleomycin-free regimen should be given to patients at higher risk 
for bleomycin-related complications (eg, patients aged >50 years, those 
with diminished renal function, those with underlying lung disease). It 
should be noted that for select cases of clinical stage IIA disease with 
borderline retroperitoneal lymph nodes, waiting 4 to 8 weeks and 
repeating imaging to confirm staging before initiating treatment can be 
considered. 

Management of Nonseminoma Stage IA, IB with and without Risk Factors, 
IIA, IIB Treated with Primary Nerve-Sparing RPLND 

Primary Treatment for Nonseminoma Stage IIB 

Treatment options following primary nerve-sparing RPLND include either 
surveillance or chemotherapy, depending on the number of positive lymph 
nodes identified. Since RPLND is likely a curative procedure in patients 
with pN0 disease, surveillance is recommended for this group. 
Surveillance is also the preferred option for patients with pN1 disease, 
although chemotherapy with two cycles of EP can also be 
considered.154,186 The risk of relapse in patients with clinical stage IIA 
nonseminoma with pN2 or pN3 disease after RPLND is >50%.154,184 This 
risk is reduced to <1% with two cycles of adjuvant cisplatin-based 
chemotherapy.154,181,183 Therefore, the NCCN Panel prefers two cycles of 
adjuvant chemotherapy with EP to surveillance for pN2 disease and 
recommends either two to three cycles of BEP or two to four cycles of EP 
for pN3 disease. As pN3 disease is a rare circumstance, the Panel could 
not reach a consensus as to the optimal regimen due to the limited data 
available. Surveillance may also be an option for patients with pN2 and 
pN3 disease and, if chosen for pN3 disease, a CT/MRI of the 
abdomen/pelvis or a chest x-ray should be conducted 2 to 3 months post-
RPLND.187 Surveillance is preferred for patients with pure teratoma. 

Follow-up for Pathologic Stage IIA/B/C Nonseminoma Undergoing 
Surveillance After Primary RPLND and Treated with Adjuvant 
Chemotherapy 

Primary treatment for patients with stage IIB nonseminoma also depends 
on post-orchiectomy tumor marker levels as well as on radiographic 
findings. When tumor marker levels are normal, the CT/MRI findings 
determine the proper course of treatment. If abnormal radiographic 
findings are limited to lymph node metastases within lymphatic drainage 
sites in the retroperitoneum (ie, the landing zone), patients may receive 
first-line chemotherapy with either three cycles of BEP or four cycles of EP 
(both preferred) or primary nerve-sparing RPLND (reserved for highly 
selected cases; ie, stage II tumors with teratoma predominance in patients 
with normal markers). RPLND is also recommended for stage II tumors 
with somatic type malignancy (previously referred to as transformed 
teratoma). Referral to a high-volume center is recommended for nerve-
sparing RPLND. Both options of first-line chemotherapy or primary nerve-
sparing RPLND are comparable in terms of outcome, but side effects and 
toxicity are different.179 The reported relapse-free survival with either 
approach is close to 98%.181-185 If metastatic disease (based on 
radiographic findings) is not confined to within the lymphatic drainage sites 
(ie, multifocal or symptomatic lymph node metastases with aberrant 
lymphatic drainage sites), first-line chemotherapy (three cycles of BEP or 
four cycles of EP; both preferred) is recommended. For patients with stage 
IIB nonseminoma with persistent marker elevation, the recommended 
treatment option is also first-line chemotherapy with either three cycles of 

Follow-up for patients after RPLND and adjuvant chemotherapy is outlined 
in Table 11 in Follow-up for Nonseminoma in the algorithm and consists of

patients who undergo RPLND and are found to have pN0 disease or pN1

Follow-up for Pathologic Stage IIA/B Nonseminoma Undergoing 
Surveillance After Primary RPLND and NOT Treated with Adjuvant 
Chemotherapy 

Follow-up for patients after RPLND and adjuvant chemotherapy is outlined 
in Table 12 in Follow-up for Nonseminoma in the algorithm and consists of 
a medical history and physical examination, serum tumor marker 
assessment, CT with contrast or MRI with and without contrast of the 
abdomen/pelvis, and chest x-ray. There is an increase in frequency of 
these tests as compared to the schedule for patients who received 
adjuvant chemotherapy due to the increase in relapse rates.188 The MRI 
protocol should include visualization of the retroperitoneal and pelvis 
nodes as well as all other nodes that need to be assessed. Chest CT with 
contrast is preferred over chest x-ray in the presence of thoracic 
symptoms. It should be noted that in patients who have pathologic stage 
IIC disease, more frequent imaging is recommended while patients who 
are found to have pN0 disease (no cancer and no teratoma, pathologic 
stage I) should revert to the surveillance schedule for low-risk NSGCT with 
the exception that only one CT is needed postoperatively around month 4.

Chemotherapy 

abdomen/pelvis CT scan with contrast or MRI with and without contrast 
within 1 month of completing chemotherapy; chest CT, MRI, or chest x-ray 
may also be considered. FDG-PET/CT scan is not clinically indicated for 
nonseminoma. Masses should be measured along the transaxial long axis 
(not the craniocaudal axis). If markers are negative and the residual mass 
is ≥1 cm after chemotherapy, nerve-sparing bilateral RPLND is 
recommended within 4 weeks of CT/MRI and within 2 weeks of 
confirmation of normal tumor markers. A bilateral RPLND involves removal 
of lymphatic tissue between both ureters, spanning from the diaphragmatic 
crus to the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries. The rationale for this 
extended region of dissection is the greater likelihood of bilateral disease 
with greater tumor burden.188 Modified template RPLND may be an option 
in select patients with initial stage IIA/B disease within the primary landing 
zones. The major morbidity associated with bilateral RPLND is retrograde 
ejaculation, resulting in infertility. Nerve-sparing dissection techniques 
preserve antegrade ejaculation in 90% of cases.189 Therefore, nerve-
sparing RPLND is recommended. For patients with negative markers and 
no residual mass or a residual mass <1 cm, surveillance is recommended; 
nerve-sparing bilateral RPLND is a category 2B recommendation in this 
setting and may be performed in selected cases, including in patients with 
subcentimeter residual nodes who have teratoma or yolk sac tumor in their 
primary tumors. These patients may be at higher risk of teratoma or viable 
GCT in the post-chemotherapy residual nodes, but more data are still 
required to know if they are at a higher risk of relapse or worse 
outcomes.190 Referral to a high-volume center is recommended for 
surgical resection of masses post-chemotherapy. If only necrotic debris or 
teratoma is present in the resected tissue, the patient should be put under 
surveillance. If embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, or seminoma 
elements are found in the residual mass, then two cycles of chemotherapy 
with either TIP, VIP, VelP, or EP is preferred. Surveillance could be 
considered as a reasonable alternative to chemotherapy for patients with

size of the residual mass on CT or MRI. Patients should thus undergo

residual masses that have been completely resected if all the residual 
masses have <10% viable cancer cells in the resected tissue. 

Follow-up for Nonseminoma Stage II–III Surveillance After Chemotherapy 
with or without Surgery 

The 5-year follow-up for patients with stage II–III nonseminoma treated 
with chemotherapy with or without RPLND can be found in Table 10 in 
Follow-up for Nonseminoma in the algorithm and includes history and 
physical examinations, serum tumor marker assessments, chest x-rays, 
and abdomen/pelvis CT scans with contrast. An MRI with and without 
contrast can be considered to replace an abdomen/pelvis CT with the 
protocol including visualization of the retroperitoneal and pelvis nodes. 
Chest x-ray may be used for routine follow-up, but chest CT with contrast 
is preferred in patients with thoracic symptoms. Annual measurement of 
serum tumor markers can be considered for years 5 through 10 following 
complete response to first-line chemotherapy in patients with metastatic 
disease.191 Additionally, patients with clinical stage II disease treated with 
chemotherapy who undergo postchemotherapy RPLND and are found to 
have pN0 disease or pN1 pure teratoma need only one CT scan at 
postoperative month 3 or 4 and then as clinically indicated while patients 
who only have a partial response to chemotherapy who are not surgical 
candidates may require more frequent imaging. 

The IGCCCG good-risk group includes patients with stages IS, IIA (S1), 
IIB (S1), IIC, and IIIA disease. The treatment goal for good-risk disease is 
to limit toxicity while maintaining maximal efficacy. Presently, two 
regimens are recommended by the NCCN Panel: three cycles of 
BEP127,129,192 or four cycles of EP128,129,192 (both category 1; both preferred). 
Both regimens are well tolerated and cure approximately 90% of patients 
with good-risk disease.192,193 The only trial that directly compared these 
two regimens found no statistically significant difference in OS (96% in the 
BEP x 3 arm vs 92% in the EP x 4 arm; P = .096) or event-free survival 
(91% with BEP x 3 vs 86% with EP x 4; P = .135).192 Factors that should 
be considered when choosing between three cycles of BEP and four 
cycles of EP include the duration of treatment (9 weeks compared to 12 
weeks) and regimen-specific toxicities (bleomycin is associated with 
reduced pulmonary function while cisplatin is associated with peripheral 
neuropathy and hearing loss). The physician and patient should make a 
shared informed decision based on patient clinical characteristics and 
preferences. A bleomycin-free regimen should be given to patients at 
higher risk for bleomycin-related complications (ie, patients aged >50 
years, those with diminished renal function, those with underlying lung 
disease). Some oncologists prefer four cycles of EP for patients who 
smoke heavily regardless of lung function. 

Advanced Metastatic Nonseminoma 

Primary Treatment for Intermediate-Risk (Stage IIIB) Nonseminoma 

The first-line chemotherapy options for patients with advanced metastatic 
nonseminoma are based on the IGCCCG risk classification, which 
categorizes patients as good, intermediate, or poor risk based on 
identification of clinically independent prognostic features such as extent 
of disease and post-orchiectomy levels of serum tumor markers.67 When 
determining a patient’s risk classification, the relevant serum tumor marker 
value is the value on Day 1 of cycle one of first-line chemotherapy. 

For patients with intermediate-risk disease, the cure rate is approximately 
70% with the standard chemotherapy regimen of four cycles of BEP.194,195 
Therefore, the NCCN Panel recommends four cycles of BEP (preferred), 
or four cycles of VIP194,196 for patients who are at higher risk for bleomycin-
related complications, for the treatment of intermediate-risk (stage IIIB) 
nonseminoma. Both regimens are category 1 recommendations. However, 
if intermediate-risk status is based solely on LDH levels 1.5 to 3 x ULN, 
then three cycles of BEP or four cycles of EP197 can be considered.

Primary Treatment for Poor-Risk (Stage IIIC) Nonseminoma 

radiographic imaging and the tumor marker levels are normal, the Panel 
recommends surveillance. Nerve-sparing bilateral RPLND can be 
considered in select cases for patients with disease that is any T, N1–3, 
and M0–1 as well as in patients with subcentimeter residual nodes who 
have teratoma or yolk sac tumor in their primary tumor (category 2B).200 
RPLND is recommended within 4 weeks of the CT scan and 2 weeks of 
marker measurement. Referral to high-volume centers is recommended 
for surgical resection of residual masses following chemotherapy. 

The standard chemotherapy regimen for poor-risk disease is four cycles of 
BEP (preferred). Alternatively, four cycles of VIP can be used to treat 
patients who are at higher risk for bleomycin-related complications.196 Both 
regimens are category 1 recommendations. However, <50% of patients 
with poor-risk nonseminoma experience a durable complete response to 
four cycles of BEP, and up to 50% die of their disease.67,198 Therefore, 
referral to a high-volume center is recommended for the treatment of 
patients with poor-risk nonseminoma.193 It should be noted that, while a 
rare circumstance, patients with poor-risk disease with choriocarcinoma-
predominant histology, very high beta-hCG, and large lung or brain 
metastases may experience hemorrhaging after initiation of 
chemotherapy. These patients should be more closely monitored and may 
require more support. 

If there is a partial radiographic response to chemotherapy (as indicated 
by the presence of residual masses) and tumor marker levels are normal, 
then surgical resection of all residual masses is recommended.201-204 As 
previously stated, referral to high-volume centers is recommended for 
surgical resection of masses post-chemotherapy. If only necrotic debris or 
teratoma is present in the resected tissue, the patient should be put under 
surveillance. If embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, or seminoma 
elements are found in the residual mass, then two cycles of chemotherapy 
with either EP, TIP, VIP, or VelP should be administered. EP should be 
considered for patients with low-volume residual disease. If there is a 
teratoma with somatic-type malignancy, consider histology-directed 
therapy and referral to a high-volume center. Surveillance can also be 
considered for patients with residual masses that have been completely 
resected if all the residual masses have <10% viable tumor cells in the 
resected tissue. 

A randomized phase II trial compared the efficacy of four cycles of BEP to 
a more intensive regimen (carboplatin, bleomycin, vincristine, and 
cisplatin/BEP [CBOP/BEP]) in 89 patients with poor-risk nonseminoma.199 
At a median follow-up of 63 months, 3-year PFS was 56% for CBOP/BEP 
and 39% for BEP (HR, 0.59; P = .079). Three-year OS was 65% and 59%, 
respectively (HR, 0.79; P = .49), and there were no differences in toxicity 
between arms. The CBOP/BEP met response targets (74% complete 
response or partial response with negative markers) and warrants further 
study in a phase III trial. 

Management of Good-, Intermediate-, and Poor-Risk Nonseminoma After 
Chemotherapy 

Further treatment for patients who experience a partial radiographic 
response to chemotherapy (residual masses) with abnormal tumor marker 
levels is guided by the kinetics of the tumor markers. Referral to a high-
volume center for residual masses with abnormal AFP and/or beta-hCG 
levels is recommended. If tumor marker levels are elevated and 
persistently rising, the Panel recommends a full course of second-line 
chemotherapy (see Second-Line Therapy below). Brain imaging and 
testicular ultrasound should be considered in patients with elevated or 

At the conclusion of first-line chemotherapy, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT 
scan with contrast/MRI with and without contrast and measurement of 
serum tumor marker levels are indicated to assess treatment response. 
FDG-PET scan has no role in assessing treatment response and residual 
masses following chemotherapy in patients with nonseminoma. If no mass 
or a residual mass <1 cm on the transaxial long axis is found by

Second-Line Therapy 

rising markers following first-line or second-line chemotherapy to evaluate 
for occult brain metastases or contralateral primary disease. Patients with 
elevated but stable marker levels should be closely surveilled. Surgery 
may be used in highly select cases in either of these patient populations 
such as with presentation of resectable retroperitoneal-only disease, 
significant factors that preclude the use of chemotherapy, and/or the 
presence of cystic components. Patients with mildly elevated and 
normalizing markers should be considered for surgical resection of 
residual masses with subsequent postoperative treatment as discussed 
above. The Panel recommends referral to a high-volume center for the 
treatment of patients with a partial response to first-line chemotherapy and 
abnormal marker levels. 

Follow-up for Good-, Intermediate-, and Poor-Risk Nonseminoma 

Patients with disease relapse following first-line therapy, or those who do 
not experience a durable complete response to first-line therapy, should 
receive second-line therapy. Patients with recurrent disease who have not 
been treated with prior chemotherapy should be treated per their risk 
status, as described in the preceding sections. Additionally, if a patient 
received prior adjuvant therapy (ie, one cycle of BEP only), first-line 
chemotherapy as previously discussed is recommended. For select 
patients with nonseminoma, RPLND may also be appropriate. It is 
preferred by the Panel that patients with recurrent seminoma or 
nonseminoma be treated at centers with expertise in the management of 
this disease. Sperm banking is also recommended if not already 
performed. While more data are still needed in this space, the Panel 
recommends that a patient should wait at least 6 months post-
chemotherapy to conceive a child or up to 2 years if using extreme 
caution. Second-line therapy options for patients with relapsed seminoma 
or early relapses (within ≤2 years of the completion of primary therapy) of 
nonseminoma include enrollment in a clinical trial, conventional-dose 
chemotherapy, or high-dose chemotherapy. If chemotherapy is given, the 
conventional-dose regimens that are preferred in this setting are TIP or 
VeIP, both of which are high risk for febrile neutropenia so G-CSFs should 
be used.144,205-207 The preferred high-dose regimens include high-dose 
carboplatin plus etoposide followed by peripheral blood stem cell 
infusion,208 or paclitaxel plus ifosfamide followed by high-dose carboplatin 
plus etoposide with stem cell support.209 Alternatively, surgery may be 
considered for nonseminoma if the recurrent mass is in a solitary 
resectable site and markers are normal or only mildly elevated.210 Late 
relapses of nonseminoma (>2 years after completion of first-line therapy) 
occur in 2% to 3% of testicular cancer survivors.211,212 The Panel prefers 

The 5-year follow-up for patients with good-, intermediate-, and poor-risk 
nonseminoma after chemotherapy (with or without post-chemotherapy 
RPLND) includes history and physical examination, serum tumor marker 
assessment, chest x-ray, and abdomen/pelvis CT with contrast or MRI 
with and without contrast. The frequency of these tests is outlined in Table 
10 in Follow-up for Nonseminoma in the algorithm. Annual measurement 
of serum tumor markers can be considered for years 5 through 10 and as 
clinically indicated thereafter following complete response to first-line 
chemotherapy in patients with metastatic disease.191 Patients who have an 
incomplete response to chemotherapy require more frequent imaging than 
is outlined in the table. Patients who undergo RPLND and are found to 
have pN0 disease or pN1 pure teratoma need only one CT scan at 
postoperative month 3 or 4 and then as clinically indicated. The MRI 
protocol should include all the nodes that need to be assessed, and chest 
x-ray may be used for routine follow-up. However, a chest CT with 
contrast is preferred in patients with thoracic symptoms, and a chest CT 
with contrast should be performed at baseline if supradiaphragmatic 
disease is present.

therapy with normal marker levels should be put under surveillance. 
Alternatively, select patients with nonseminoma may receive nerve-
sparing bilateral RPLND (category 2B), followed by surveillance. Referral 
to a high-volume center is recommended for nerve-sparing RPLND. For 
patients with nonseminoma and a partial response to second-line therapy 
(as indicated by residual masses on CT scan) and normal marker levels, 
surgical resection of all residual masses is recommended followed by 
surveillance. If there is a teratoma with somatic-type malignancy, consider 
histology-directed therapy and referral to a high-volume center. Patients 
with a partial response to second-line therapy (residual masses) and 
abnormal marker levels should be treated according to the kinetics of the 
tumor markers. If tumor marker levels are elevated and persistently rising, 
the Panel recommends third-line therapy (see Third-Line Therapy below). 
Patients with elevated but stable tumor marker levels should be closely 
surveilled. Patients with mildly elevated and normalizing markers should 
be considered for surgical resection of residual masses followed by 
surveillance. Referral to high-volume centers is recommended for surgical 
resection of residual masses following chemotherapy. 

An ongoing, randomized, international, phase III trial (TIGER) will compare 
second-line conventional-dose chemotherapy with high-dose 
chemotherapy in patients with relapsed GCTs.213 The foundation of the 
TIGER trial was formed based on the results of a large retrospective 
analysis by Lorch et al, which demonstrated the superiority of carboplatin-
based high-dose chemotherapy compared to cisplatin-based conventional-
dose chemotherapy with respect to 2-year PFS (50% vs 28%; P < .001) 
and 5-year OS (53% vs 41%; P < .001).214,215 The TIGER trial will 
randomize patients with unequivocal disease progression following 
cisplatin-based first-line chemotherapy to receive conventional-dose TIP 
or high-dose paclitaxel plus ifosfamide followed by high-dose carboplatin 
plus etoposide with stem cell support. OS is the primary endpoint. 
Secondary endpoints include PFS, response rate, toxicity, quality of life, 
and biological correlates.213,214 This trial has completed patient recruitment 
and results are expected sometime in the near future (Clinical Trial ID: 
NCT02375204). 

Third-Line Therapy 

Management of Metastatic Germ Cell Tumors After Second-Line Therapy 

To assess response after second-line therapy, a CT scan with contrast or 
MRI with and without contrast of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and any 
other sites of disease is recommended. FDG-PET/CT scan has no role in 
assessing treatment response and residual masses following 
chemotherapy in patients with nonseminoma but could be considered in 
assessing treatment response and residual masses following 
chemotherapy in patients with seminoma. Levels of serum tumor markers 
should also be measured. For patients with seminoma, follow-up is similar 
to post first-line chemotherapy treatment discussed above. Patients with 

Third-line therapy is recommended for patients with progressive disease 
(growing mass or rising markers) or recurrent disease following second-
line therapy. In order to maintain optimal efficacy and limit treatment-
related toxicities, the chemotherapy regimens previously received by the 
patient should be considered when deciding on third-line therapy options. 
Participation in a clinical trial is the preferred treatment option for patients 
who experience relapse and have received prior high-dose chemotherapy. 
Alternatively, for patients previously treated with conventional-dose 
chemotherapy, high-dose regimens are preferred. For those patients with 
seminoma, conventional-dose third-line chemotherapy can be considered 
regardless of previous treatment and RT can be considered in select

phase II study of patients with treatment-resistant GCTs also found the 
combination of gemcitabine, oxaliplatin, and paclitaxel to be effective with 
acceptable toxicity.216 The overall response rate was 51% with 5% of 
patients achieving a complete response. A second study reported similar 
results.222 Additionally, high-dose single-agent oral etoposide was shown 
to be effective in a phase II study involving patients who had previous 
treatment with cisplatin/etoposide combination regimens.223 

patients. Patients previously treated with either high-dose or conventional-
dose regimens may also undergo surgical treatment (if solitary resectable 
site). Molecular testing, including both next-generation sequencing and 
immunohistochemistry, is recommended to determine eligibility for pan-
cancer, tumor-agnostic biomarker-directed therapies as these therapies 
can be considered for patients with actionable mutations. For patients with 
nonseminoma, surgical treatment for a solitary site can be considered 
regardless of previous therapy. Conventional-dose third-line 
chemotherapy may be given to patients who received prior high-dose 
chemotherapy. Molecular testing should similarly be performed in patients 
with nonseminoma who have either received or are not eligible for high-
dose chemotherapy to determine eligibility for pan-cancer, tumor-agnostic, 
biomarker-directed therapies. Furthermore, for patients with nonseminoma 
who experience a late relapse (>2 years after completion of second-line 
therapy), the preferred treatment option is surgery if the recurrent mass is 
resectable. Conventional-dose or high-dose chemotherapy (if not 
previously received) are also options for patients with late relapse. 

High-dose chemotherapy regimens for third-line therapy are the same as 
those discussed for second-line treatment (see above). The recommended 
third-line palliative chemotherapy options for patients with intensively 
pretreated, cisplatin-resistant, or refractory GCTs are combinations of 
gemcitabine with paclitaxel and/or oxaliplatin,216-222 or oral etoposide.223 
The recommendation for gemcitabine and oxaliplatin (GEMOX) is based 
on data from phase II studies investigating the efficacy and toxicity of 
GEMOX in patients with relapsed or cisplatin-resistant GCTs.217,219,221 
These studies showed that GEMOX is safe for patients with 
cisplatin-resistant testicular GCTs and may enhance long-term disease-
free survival.217,219,221 Gemcitabine plus paclitaxel is another option that 
has shown promising results in a phase II study.218 Follow-up results 
showed long-term DFS in patients who progressed after high-dose 
chemotherapy and had not received prior paclitaxel or gemcitabine.220 A 

Studies on other regimens in this setting have also been published, such 
as one retrospective study of 22 men that showed treatment with 
paclitaxel/cisplatin/gemcitabine led to partial remissions in 8 patients 
(36%) with the median (range) OS being 13.5 months.224 Grade 3–4 
thrombocytopenia and neutropenia were observed in 15 patients (68%) 
and anemia in 9 patients (41%).224 Four patients (18%) were long-term 
disease-free survivors after a minimum of a 6-year follow-up.224 
Additionally, in a phase II study that evaluated a different regimen, 
cisplatin/epirubicin, 30 patients with metastatic GCT who had received at 
least one previous cisplatin-based regimen were enrolled, 19 of which 
received all 4 cycles.225 Nine patients achieved complete remission, and 
hematologic toxicities were most commonly observed.225 Moreover, in 
another retrospective institutional experience by Xiang et al, the regimen, 
doxorubicin/paclitaxel/cisplatin, was evaluated in 35 patients (24 of which 
were treated with nonpalliative intent while 11 were treated with palliative 
intent) and showed an objective response rate of 37.5% (1 complete 
response and 8 partial responses) in the nonpalliative intent cohort with a 
median PFS of 4.3 months and a median OS of 13.1 months.226 For 
patients in the palliative intent cohort, 1 partial response was observed 
(objective response rate of 9%) with the median PFS and median OS 
being 0.92 months and 5.2 months, respectively.226 Treatment toxicities 
that required a dose reduction were observed in 5 patients (14%), and 
myelosuppression was observed most commonly in those patients who 
were admitted for treatment-related toxicities.226 At this time, these

acknowledges that these regimens may be useful in certain, rare

Treatment of Brain Metastases 

The optimal management of brain metastases from testicular GCTs is 
controversial, with a lack of evidence from prospective trials to guide 
treatment decisions.227,229 Therefore, management decisions are usually 
based on institutional preferences, which may in part explain the large 
variation in treatment modalities received by these patients. The NCCN 
Guidelines recommend first-line cisplatin-based chemotherapy 
(chemotherapy for poor-risk disease) for patients with brain metastases. 
The addition of RT to chemotherapy regimens can also be considered.232 
Surgical resection of metastatic brain lesions should be performed if 
clinically indicated and feasible. A recent retrospective analysis reported 
the treatment of 25 patients with relapsed GCTs and progressive brain 
metastases who received multimodality therapy, which included high-dose 
chemotherapy with stem cell support alone or combined with surgery 
and/or stereotactic or whole-brain RT.233 At a median follow-up of 24.5 
months, 44% of patients were alive with no evidence of disease, 
suggesting that this subset of patients with historically poor prognosis can 

Brain metastases from testicular GCTs are relatively rare and occur 
almost exclusively in patients with nonseminoma histology.227 The 
development of brain metastases may be more common in patients with a 
higher burden of systemic disease; lung, liver, and/or bone metastases; 
high levels of serum beta-hCG (>5000 IU/L); in those with neurologic 
symptoms; and in those who experience relapse after cisplatin-based 
chemotherapy. The prognosis of patients with brain metastases from 
testicular GCTs is poor, with >50% of patients dying within 1 year of 
diagnosis.227,228 Patients with additional adverse prognostic factors, 
especially those with metachronous brain metastases, have even worse 
outcomes.227,229,230 

potentially be cured with this approach. 

Malignant Transformation of Teratoma 

In a retrospective analysis, Loriot et al reported on the pattern of relapse 
among patients with poor-risk nonseminomatous GCTs previously treated 
with chemotherapy.231 After a median follow-up of 4.1 years, 32% were 
found to have radiographic evidence of brain metastases. The brain was 
the only site of progression in 54% of these patients and 19% experienced 
progression in the brain as the first progression event. Furthermore, 
involvement of the brain was more common among patients who were 
previously treated with high-dose chemotherapy (29%) compared to BEP 
(12%). These data suggest that brain metastases from testicular GCTs 
may occur more frequently than previously thought, often as the only site 
of progression, and may be more likely to occur in patients at poor risk 
previously treated with high-dose chemotherapy. However, it is unknown 
whether this effect was due to the lower cerebral drug penetrance of the 
high-dose regimen. 

Teratoma is a pluripotent tissue that has the capacity to dedifferentiate into 
somatic malignancies. Sarcomas or carcinomas arising from teratoma are 
generally resistant to chemotherapy and are associated with poor 
prognosis.55,234-236 Somatic transformation of teratoma is most frequently 
seen in patients with metastatic disease who have been treated with 
chemotherapy. However, this can occasionally be seen in patients who 
have not received chemotherapy as well. Given the insensitivity of these 
tumors to systemic chemotherapy, surgical resection is the preferred 
treatment if feasible. RPLND should be considered in patients with stage I 
disease who have teratoma with malignant transformation in their primary 
tumor in order to eradicate any microscopic retroperitoneal metastases 
and reduce the risk of relapse. For patients with more advanced disease 
(stage II or III), complete surgical resection if feasible is preferred. For

treatment strategies. The ongoing international phase III TIGER trial aims 
to determine whether high-dose or conventional-dose chemotherapy is 
more effective in the second-line setting for patients with relapsed disease. 
Patients with platinum-refractory or relapsing tumors after second-line 
therapy have very poor outcomes despite subsequent-line treatments with 
no effective alternative therapies. Targeted therapies appear to have 
limited activity in this setting, although more robust clinical trials are 
needed to assess their value in treating testicular GCTs. Prognosis for 
patients with brain metastases remains poor, with a lack of evidence from 
prospective trials to guide treatment decisions. Therefore, the NCCN 
Panel encourages patients with metastatic, recurrent, or platinum-
refractory testicular GCTs to participate in well-designed clinical trials 
investigating novel therapeutic strategies to enable further advances for 
the management of this disease. 

 

Malignant transformation of teratoma along mesodermal lines results in a 
primitive small round blue cell tumor referred to as embryonic-type 
neuroectodermal tumor (ENT).237 This was previously termed primitive 
neuroectodermal tumor (PNET) arising from teratoma. The preferred 
modality of therapy for malignant transformation of teratoma to ENT is also 
surgical resection. ENT transformed from teratoma is resistant to cisplatin-
based chemotherapy. Chemotherapy directed to ENT histology is 
associated with objective response. The preferred regimen consists of 
cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and vincristine (CAV) alternating with 
ifosfamide plus etoposide (IE).238 For patients with stage I disease with 
ENT histology, RPLND should be considered. If ENT histology is present 
in surgical resection specimen, adjuvant chemotherapy with CAV 
alternating with IE for a total of four cycles should be considered. 238,239 
Rarely, GCTs may originate in extragonadal sites (usually the 
retroperitoneum or mediastinum). Patients with an extragonadal primary 
site are treated similarly to patients with testicular GCTs regarding 
systemic therapies and management of residual masses.240 However, due 
to their rarity, the NCCN Panel recommends that patients with 
extragonadal GCTs be referred to high-volume centers with experience in 
managing these tumors. 

Summary 

The NCCN Guidelines for Testicular Cancer provide an evidence- and 
consensus-based treatment approach for the treatment of adult patients 
with seminomatous and nonseminomatous testicular GCTs. Testicular 
GCTs are sensitive to platinum-based chemotherapy and patients have 
high cure rates even with metastatic disease. Although the majority of 
metastatic testicular GCTs are cured with chemotherapy, 20% to 30% of 
patients will relapse after first-line chemotherapy and require additional

Elevations of AFP either pre- or post-orchiectomy indicate the presence of nonseminomatous elements. The expected half-life for AFP is 5–7 days. For patients with elevated pre-orchiectomy beta-hCG levels, beta-hCG levels should be followed with repeated determinations after orchiectomy to determine their trajectory and, if declining, their nadir. The expected half-life for beta-hCG is ≤3 days. For patients with normal imaging (ie, stage I), rising or persistently elevated beta-hCG levels generally indicate the presence of metastatic disease (stage IS). suspicious_testicular_mass.definition: The case describes a suspicious testicular mass as the presenting finding.

histology.definition: Histologic type of the primary testicular tumor as reported by pathology.

afp_level.definition: Serum AFP category as stated in the case (normal, mildly elevated, elevated). not_available if not measured.

hcg_level.definition: Serum beta-hCG category as stated in the case (normal, mildly elevated, elevated). not_available if not measured.

ldh_level.definition: Serum LDH category as stated in the case. not_available if not measured.

afp_trend.definition: Direction of serial AFP values over time as stated in the case. not_applicable if only one value exists.

hcg_trend.definition: Direction of serial beta-hCG values over time as stated in the case. not_applicable if only one value exists.

post_orchiectomy_marker_measurements_cou.definition: Number of serial AFP and/or beta-hCG measurements recorded after orchiectomy, as stated in the case. 0 if none.

post_orchiectomy_marker_elevated_measure.definition: Number of the post-orchiectomy AFP or beta-hCG measurements that the case states as elevated (mildly elevated or elevated). 0 if none.

persistent_marker_elevation_stated.definition: The case explicitly states that tumor markers (AFP and/or beta-hCG) remain elevated after orchiectomy (persistent marker elevation).

primary_treatment.definition: Initial treatment actually given to the patient for the primary tumor or nodal disease.

pt_category.definition: Pathologic T category of the primary testicular tumor.

pn_category.definition: Pathologic N category from retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.

m_category.definition: Distant metastasis category as stated in the case.

s_category.definition: Serum tumor marker (S) category as stated in the case staging summary.

retroperitoneal_mass_cm.definition: Largest diameter of the retroperitoneal nodal mass before any treatment, on CT or MRI. 0 if no nodal mass.

residual_mass_cm.definition: Largest residual mass diameter after chemotherapy, transaxial long axis, on CT or MRI. 0 if no residual mass.

residual_mass_growing.definition: A residual or known mass is growing on serial imaging, as stated in the case.

lymphovascular_invasion.definition: Lymphovascular invasion is present in the primary tumor, as reported by pathology.

embryonal_carcinoma_predominant.definition: Embryonal carcinoma is the predominant component of the primary tumor, as reported by pathology.

brain_metastases.definition: Brain metastases are present, as stated in the case.

mediastinal_primary.definition: The primary germ cell tumor is located in the mediastinum.

multifocal_tumor.definition: Multifocal disease is present, as stated in the case.

symptomatic_at_presentation.definition: The patient presents with symptoms attributable to metastatic disease, as stated in the case.

lymph_node_metastasis_site.definition: Location of lymph node metastases relative to expected lymphatic drainage, as stated in the case.

pet_result.definition: FDG-PET/CT result for residual disease after chemotherapy.

weeks_since_chemotherapy_end.definition: Time in weeks from the end of the most recent chemotherapy to the current assessment.

residual_histology.definition: Histology of resected or biopsied residual mass after chemotherapy.

resection_status.definition: Extent of surgical management of the residual mass.

prior_treatment_line.definition: Most advanced prior systemic treatment line the patient has received.

stem_cell_rescue_received.definition: The patient has received a stem cell rescue (autologous stem cell transplant) after prior chemotherapy, as stated in the case.

high_dose_chemotherapy_stated_in_case.definition: The case explicitly states that prior chemotherapy was high-dose.

years_since_primary_treatment_end.definition: Years from completion of primary treatment to the relapse or current assessment.

years_since_second_line_end.definition: Years from completion of second-line therapy to the relapse or current assessment.

guideline_section.definition: Which disease or subtype section of this guideline the case belongs to: the disease named in the guideline's page headings that the patient has (e.g. the tumor type or subtype).

treatment_phase.definition: Phase of care at the decision now, as named by the guideline page heading (e.g. STAGE IIA, IIB, IIC, III AFTER FIRST LINE TREATMENT WITH CHEMOTHERAPY; FOLLOW-UP) or as stated in the case. other if none applies.

germ_cell_category.definition: Pure seminoma requires seminoma histology with normal AFP. NSGCT includes mixed tumors, nonseminomatous histology, and seminoma histology with elevated AFP.

n_category.definition: Retroperitoneal nodal category from the largest nodal mass diameter before treatment, using the box size thresholds (<3 cm, 3-5 cm).

stage_group.definition: Stage group at diagnosis from pathologic T, nodal category, M category and S category, using the stage groups printed in the boxes.

nsgct_stage_i_risk_factors.definition: Stage I NSGCT risk factors: lymphovascular invasion and/or embryonal carcinoma predominance.

markers_negative.definition: All tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) are normal.

progressive_disease.definition: Progressive disease: a growing mass or rising markers.

marker_pattern.definition: Pattern of abnormal tumor markers during follow-up after chemotherapy.

afp_elevated_and_rising.definition: Elevated and rising AFP, as printed in the box 'Elevated and rising AFP'. Does not count a rising beta-hCG.

nsgct_response.definition: Response of NSGCT after chemotherapy from markers and residual mass size (1 cm threshold).

seminoma_post_chemo_category.definition: Seminoma residual disease category after chemotherapy (3 cm threshold with normal AFP and beta-hCG).

seminoma_residual_management.definition: Pathway after resection or biopsy of residual seminoma-containing mass.

incomplete_resection_or_progression.definition: Incomplete resection or progression, as printed in the box 'Incomplete resection or Progression'. A positive biopsy alone does not count.

seminoma_rt_dose_by_nodal_size.definition: Radiotherapy dose band by nodal mass size before treatment, as printed in the box: 30 Gy for 1-2 cm, 36 Gy for 2-3 cm. A mass of exactly 2 cm is printed in both bands and is returned as exactly_2_cm so the box is not encoded on an invented boundary.

nsgct_original_stage_branch.definition: Branch on the stage at diagnosis for NSGCT patients with residual masses after chemotherapy.

germ_cell_risk_group.criteria_source: external: NCCN Risk Classification for Advanced Disease (TEST-D)
germ_cell_risk_group.definition: Germ cell risk group for advanced disease, from stage, M category, brain metastases and mediastinal primary.

intermediate_or_poor_risk_as_printed.definition: Advanced NSGCT stage IIIB or IIIC, as printed in the follow-up box 'Intermediate risk and poor risk: Stage IIIB, IIIC'. Narrower than germ_cell_risk_group, which also covers M1a, M1b, brain and mediastinal cases; use this one where the box is encoded.

early_relapse_after_primary_treatment.definition: Relapse occurred 2 years or less after completion of primary treatment.

late_relapse_after_second_line.definition: Relapse occurred more than 2 years after completion of second-line chemotherapy.

conventional_dose_first_and_second_line.definition: Prior first- and second-line chemotherapy both given at conventional dose: second-line therapy recorded and no high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell rescue. Does not test late relapse.

nsgct_nodal_pattern.definition: Pattern of nodal metastases for NSGCT with markers negative.

markers_persistently_elevated.definition: Tumor markers (AFP and/or beta-hCG) remain elevated on repeated measurements after orchiectomy. True if the case explicitly states persistent marker elevation, or if two or more post-orchiectomy measurements are stated as elevated. The boxes do not state a numeric criterion for 'persistent' or 'repeated'; the two-measurement reading is an assumption of this schema.

prior_high_dose_chemotherapy.definition: The patient has previously received high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell rescue. True if the case explicitly states high-dose chemotherapy, or if a stem cell rescue was received.

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
